introduction: The guide holds two statements together. The first is that creation is perfect: a tree needs leaves as well as fruit, each kingdom is complete in its own station, and “there is naught in creation more wondrous than that which already exists.” The second is that nature is defective: untended land grows thorns, the struggle for existence is its law, and human beings must be educated out of it. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s way between them is to ask “perfect in relation to what?” Paul’s body with many members, the psalms, Marcus Aurelius, Pope and Hopkins’s dappled things speak for the first statement; Proverbs’ neglected field, Tennyson and Huxley for the second. Each has its critics. Voltaire, after Lisbon, would not hear that whatever is, is right. Darwin, Thoreau and Hopkins found in the tangled bank and the wilderness something that cultivation would destroy, and Mencius thought human nature needs clearing, not correcting.
questions: “God is pure perfection and the creation is absolute imperfection,” yet “in the creation of God there is no defect,” and Genesis calls everything very good. How does the idea of relative perfection reconcile these?
Voltaire asked how a “general bliss” could be composed from individuals’ woes. Does the saying that nothing is more wondrous than what exists claim what he attacks?

The readings picture wild land as a dark jungle; Thoreau says “in Wildness is the preservation of the World,” and Hopkins prays for the weeds. What are the readings using nature as an image of, and what do these writers add?
“All sin is prompted by the dictates of nature,” though the same impulses are no sin in an animal. Jesus says evil comes out of the heart. Where would you locate the source of wrongdoing?
Greed and anger are praiseworthy when rightly directed, and Aristotle says that directing them rightly is the hard part. What does this imply about how character is educated?
There is “always a point ahead.” Is unending imperfection a discouraging thought or, as Browning has it, what a heaven is for?

outside.why: The mineral “has no right to object” that it was not made a plant. Paul uses the potter: shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus?
“If this tree were to become entirely fruit” there would be no tree. Paul on the body: if the whole body were an eye, where were the hearing? If they were all one member, where were the body?

Beauty requires “the ear, the eye, the brain, and even the nails and hair.” Marcus Aurelius: we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth.
The Báb quotes this verse of the Qur’án for the perfection of each thing in its station: surely We created man of the best stature.
The world of man is “a world of perfection in relation to that of things.” The eighth psalm: a little lower than the angels, with dominion over the works of thy hands.
A masterpiece shows its painter’s skill and still falls short of the painter. The Wisdom of Solomon: by the greatness and beauty of the creatures proportionably the maker of them is seen.
“God is pure perfection.” Jesus refuses a compliment on the same ground: there is none good but one, that is, God.

“The creation is absolute imperfection.” The first chapter of Genesis ends on a different note: God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. Is the difference one of doctrine or of the standard used?
No created thing is such “that nothing superior to it can be imagined.” Browning’s painter says why that is good news: a man’s reach should exceed his grasp, or what’s a heaven for?

“Every seed has, from the beginning, all the perfections of the plant.” A father in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad has his son split a fig seed and find nothing in it: of that subtle essence which you do not perceive, this great tree exists.
Perfections “only become apparent gradually.” Jesus’s parable of the seed growing secretly: first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.
“There is naught in creation more wondrous than that which already exists.” Pope’s Essay on Man reaches the same verdict in six words: whatever is, is right.
All things are “arranged, composed, ordered.” John Muir found the order by trying to isolate one thing: we find it hitched to everything else in the universe.

Nothing more wondrous than what already is. After the earthquake that destroyed Lisbon in 1755, Voltaire asked the optimists whether they would compose a general bliss from individuals’ woes. What must the saying mean if it is to survive his question?
“The absolute order and perfection of creation.” A psalm on the same survey: O Lord, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all.
A universal power “directing and regulating all the parts.” Marcus Aurelius: constantly regard the universe as one living being, having one substance and one soul.
All beings “mutually influence one another.” Emerson: all are needed by each one; nothing is fair or good alone.
“The individuality of each created thing is based upon divine wisdom.” Hopkins gives glory for dappled things, and all things counter, original, spare, strange.
In creation are “the signs of ancient wisdom and power.” Proverbs: the Lord by wisdom hath founded the earth; by understanding hath he established the heavens.
The grower is impressed more and more by the “ever expansive varieties of plants.” Jesus: consider the lilies of the field; even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
The bee is “a perfect architect” without study. Proverbs sends the idler to another such creature: go to the ant, which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, provideth her meat in the summer.
Man’s function is “to rescue and redeem himself from the inherent defects of nature.” Huxley, Darwin’s champion, said the same in 1893: ethical progress depends on combating the cosmic process.

Atoms mingle and life results; then comes the human task. Rúmí’s ascent passes through the same kingdoms: I died as mineral and became a plant, I died as plant and rose to animal, I died as animal and I was man.
Bahá’u’lláh’s wayfarer exclaims a verse of the Qur’án. This is its setting, in the chapter of the Sovereignty: thou canst see no fault in the Beneficent One’s creation; then look again.
“We must therefore labour to destroy the animal condition.” Tennyson: move upward, working out the beast, and let the ape and tiger die.
Land left to itself is “covered with thorns and thistles.” Proverbs passed such a field and drew its lesson from the nettles and the broken wall.

Thorns, thistles and useless weeds are the natural state. Genesis treats them as a consequence and not as the first design: cursed is the ground for thy sake; thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee.

A piece of wild land is “a jungle,” dark and imperfect. Darwin stops before an entangled bank, with its birds, insects and worms, and finds it interesting to contemplate, and in the end grand. Are he and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá looking at the same thing?
Uncultivated nature is the picture of incompleteness. Thoreau, walking west out of Concord, staked everything on it: in Wildness is the preservation of the World.

“Useless weeds and wild vegetation.” Hopkins, a priest, by a Highland stream: what would the world be, once bereft of wet and of wildness? Long live the weeds and the wilderness yet. What would he say is lost when everything is cultivated?
Nature is defective, and so man needs “divine education and inspiration.” Aquinas keeps the two orders in one sentence: grace does not destroy nature but perfects it.

It is “an essential condition” of the soil that thorns grow from it. Mencius held that human nature inclines to good as water runs downhill, and that evil has to be forced on it. Does the garden image fit what you have seen of people?
“Nature is the source of vices”; man is the founder of virtues. Isaiah’s parable has a vineyard given every care that still brought forth wild grapes.
Nature unassisted is “a plane upon which the struggle for physical existence expresses itself.” Tennyson, nine years before Darwin’s book, had the phrase for it: Nature, red in tooth and claw.

The divine philosophers admit the grandeur of “the colossal suns and planets” and still call nature incomplete. Kant sets the starry heavens above him beside the moral law within him, which alone raises his worth.

“The materialists hold to the opinion that the world of nature is complete.” Darwin, often counted among them, did not say complete; he said that endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved. Is that the opinion the reading rejects?
Nature “seems perfect” and is not the last word. Paul: that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural; and afterward that which is spiritual.
“A jungle of disorder and confusion … producing nothing but fruitless, useless trees.” Hamlet on the world as he finds it: ’tis an unweeded garden, that grows to seed.
Nature “is almost chaotic, until man inspired of the Spirit comes to direct her.” Bacon’s rule for the directing: nature to be commanded must be obeyed. Which laws does the electric light obey?

Greed and anger are praiseworthy “under the right circumstances.” Aristotle: anyone can get angry, that is easy; but to do this to the right person, to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive, is not for everyone.
“In the innate nature of things there is no evil - all is good.” Henry V on the eve of battle: there is some soul of goodness in things evil, would men observingly distil it out.
The dictates of nature are sins in man though not in the animal. Paul feels them as another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá reinterprets the inheritance of Adam’s sin as attachment to the material world. This is the sentence of Paul on which the older doctrine rests: by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin.
The condition “was inherited by His descendants.” Ezekiel refuses inherited guilt in any form: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. Is a tendency inherited the same thing as a guilt?

Lying, tyranny and deceit are “characteristic of the world of nature.” Jesus traces them to a nearer source: out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, thefts, false witness. Is “nature” outside the human heart or in it?
“Evil is imperfection.” Augustine: evil has no positive nature; the loss of good has received the name evil.
Defects are “merely the absence of virtues and the lack of perfections.” Augustine again, in his handbook: what is that which we call evil but the absence of good?
Through disobedience “the sun of Thy gifts has shone forth.” Paul’s daring sentence: where sin abounded, grace did much more abound.
Nature’s world of defects, or the Kingdom reached “by the highway of Religion.” Moses’s last charge sets out two ways: I have set before you life and death; therefore choose life.
Earth “is the crucible for refining and moulding character.” Job: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.

To attain one’s perfection is paradise; to fail of it is hell. Milton gives a near thought to Satan, who means it as defiance: the mind is its own place, and in itself can make a heaven of hell, a hell of heaven. What separates the two uses of the idea?
“The degree of Perfection reached by a thing is its Paradise.” Khayyám’s soul comes back from the invisible with a similar report and no programme: I myself am Heaven and Hell.
Each thing has “the highest point possible for it.” Paul: there is one glory of the sun, and another of the moon; one star differeth from another star in glory.

thoreau-in-wildness.text: The West of which I speak is but another name for the Wild; and what I have been preparing to say is, that in Wildness is the preservation of the World
thoreau-in-wildness.author: Henry David Thoreau

hopkins-weeds-and-the-wilderness.text: What would the world be, once bereft / Of wet and of wildness? Let them be left, / O let them be left, wildness and wet; / Long live the weeds and the wilderness yet
hopkins-weeds-and-the-wilderness.author: Gerard Manley Hopkins

genesis-thorns-and-thistles.text: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life; Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field
